title: Erdős #606: Why the Forbidden Line Counts Are Exactly C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3

problemStatement.formal: Why are the forbidden line counts exactly C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3, and no others? Placing k of the points on a common line collapses their C(k,2) pairs to a single line, dropping the line count by the deficit C(k,2)−1: 0 for an ordinary 2-point line, 2 for a triple, 5 for a quadruple. Using disjoint such groups, every achievable total deficit is a non-negative combination of these deficits — in particular of 2 (triples) and 5 (quadruples). Which deficits, hence which top-range line counts, are unreachable?
problemStatement.plain: The arithmetic core of the Erdős–Salamon gap structure: the two unreachable distinct-line counts are exactly the Frobenius gaps {1,3} of the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩, where 2 and 5 are the line-count deficits of a collinear triple and quadruple.

insights: The two Erdős–Salamon gaps are not an accident of the geometry but a shadow of a classical number-theoretic fact: the numerical semigroup generated by 2 and 5 has Frobenius number 3 and gap set exactly {1, 3}.

The generators 2 and 5 are the smallest positive line-count deficits: a collinear triple (C(3,2)−1 = 2) and a collinear quadruple (C(4,2)−1 = 5). Every other deficit is built from these, so triples and quadruples alone suffice to realize every non-forbidden value.

Deficit 1 is impossible because a single rich line already removes at least 2 lines (3 pairs → 1 line); deficit 3 is impossible because 3 is not a non-negative combination of 2 and 5. These are precisely the C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3 gaps.

This file is purely the arithmetic core: it does not claim the geometric realizability of the configurations (that disjoint triples/quadruples embed in the plane), which is the genuine geometric content axiomatized in the parent, nor does it resolve the open threshold N₀.
